question: What is a mushroom?
teaser: The red toadstool in the park is only the fruit. Find the rest of the fungus, and the trees it trades with.

stops.title: A fly agaric
text: This red toadstool with white warts is a fly agaric. It is poisonous, so never eat a wild mushroom you cannot identify with certainty. It is not a plant: a fungus has no chlorophyll and cannot make food from light, it absorbs its food, and genetically it is closer kin to animals. And what you see is not the whole organism.
stops.model: A procedural model of a typical fly agaric. The cap diameter here, 14 cm, was chosen within the species range of about 5 to 30 cm.
stops.notice: Look around the park: the mushroom is near the trees. That is not an accident, as the last stops show.

stops.title: Gills under the cap
text: Cut in half, the cap shows thin white plates fanned out beneath it, called gills. Each plate is lined on both sides with cells that make spores.
Many thin plates give far more surface for spores than a flat underside would.
stops.notice: Count the gills where the cut passes through them.

stops.title: Spores
text: A spore is a single cell, far smaller than a seed. Fly agaric spores are white and oval, about 9 to 13 micrometres long. A spore that lands somewhere good can grow threads of a new fungus, and two compatible threads must meet before a mushroom can form. A mushroom sheds a huge number of spores, and almost all of them die.
stops.notice: Find where the spores form on the surface of a gill.

stops.title: The hidden fungus
text: Under the ground is the fungus itself: a web of fine threads called the mycelium. The mushroom is its fruit, which it builds to release spores, the way an apple tree makes apples.
The mycelium can be far bigger than the mushroom, and it lasts longer.
stops.model: The white threads are drawn several hundred times too thick to be seen. Real threads are only about 2 to 10 micrometres wide.
stops.notice: Follow the threads to the tree roots on the right.

stops.title: The partnership
text: The fungus wraps the finest tree roots in a sleeve of threads, and grows between the root's outer cells, but not inside them. The tree pays in sugar, and the fungus pays in water, nitrogen and phosphate. In one study of ectomycorrhizal fungi in Arctic tundra, the fungi received about 8 to 17 percent of the plants' photosynthetic carbon and supplied about 61 to 86 percent of their nitrogen.
stops.model: The root tips are drawn much larger than life so that you can see them.
stops.notice: Find the sleeve around the root and the threads running out into the soil.

answer: A mushroom is the short-lived fruit of a fungus whose real body is a web of fine threads in the soil, and which often trades minerals and water for sugar with the roots of trees.
unknown: How much sugar and how many minerals actually pass between a fungus and a tree in the wild varies a lot, and the exact amounts are still being measured.
